claims.text: The patient presented to the emergency department on 05/01/26 with sudden severe central chest pain rated 8/10, exacerbated by deep breaths and movement, with onset approximately one hour prior to arrival.
Associated symptoms included mild shortness of breath; the patient denied haemoptysis, nausea, vomiting, palpitations, syncope, dysphagia, dysuria, haematuria, dizziness, or focal weakness.
Past medical history includes asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis.
The patient has a known allergy to pollen.
The patient reported no current medications at presentation.
Social history indicates the patient lives alone, is independent with activities of daily living, works as an IT consultant, and is a non-smoker with no alcohol or recreational drug use.
Family history is reported as nil significant.

Initial observations on 05/01/26 recorded a heart rate of 110 bpm, blood pressure of 135/85 mmHg, respiratory rate of 24/min, temperature of 37.1°C, and SpO2 of 96% on room air (noted as 95% in one record).

Physical examination on 05/01/26 revealed mild tenderness over the sternum/anterior chest wall and palpable subcutaneous crepitus in the neck and chest; lung auscultation showed equal air entry with no added sounds.
An ECG performed at 02:30 on 05/01/26 showed sinus tachycardia with no ischaemic changes.
A chest X-ray performed on 05/01/26 confirmed spontaneous pneumomediastinum and subcutaneous emphysema, with no evidence of pneumothorax.
The clinical impression was spontaneous pneumomediastinum, likely secondary to a recent coughing episode or straining, with no evidence of haemodynamic instability.
Management on 05/01/26 included admission to the respiratory high-dependency unit, paracetamol 1g QDS PRN for pain, and ibuprofen 400mg TDS for pain.
The patient was advised to avoid straining, heavy lifting, or activities that increase intrathoracic pressure.

A physiotherapy session on 05/01/26 at 11:00 focused on diaphragmatic breathing and pursed-lip breathing; observations at that time showed a heart rate of 88 bpm, blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg, respiratory rate of 20/min, and SpO2 of 96% on room air.

On 05/01/26, observations showed a heart rate of 88 bpm, blood pressure of 130/80 mmHg, respiratory rate of 18/min, and SpO2 of 97% on room air; examination noted no subcutaneous emphysema on palpation and no respiratory distress.
Omeprazole 20mg OD was started on 05/01/26 to prevent gastrointestinal side effects from ibuprofen.
A repeat chest X-ray on 06/01/26 showed a slight reduction in pneumomediastinum compared to initial imaging.

A physiotherapy session on 06/01/26 at 12:00 noted subcutaneous emphysema with no evidence of spread; observations included a heart rate of 88 bpm, blood pressure of 130/80 mmHg, respiratory rate of 18/min, and SpO2 of 97% on room air.
On 07/01/26, the patient reported no chest pain overnight and mild improvement in breathing comfort; examination showed no palpable subcutaneous crepitus.
Regular paracetamol and ibuprofen were stopped on 07/01/26 as the patient was pain-free.
A repeat chest X-ray was planned for 48 hours after 07/01/26 to assess further resolution.
On 07/01/26, the patient received education regarding signs of pneumomediastinum recurrence and when to seek urgent medical attention post-discharge.

On 08/01/26, observations showed a heart rate of 82 bpm, blood pressure of 128/78 mmHg, respiratory rate of 16/min, temperature of 36.8°C, and SpO2 of 97% on air; examination was normal with no subcutaneous crepitus.
A chest X-ray on 08/01/26 showed no complications and stable pneumomediastinum with continued improvement.
Discharge planning was initiated on 08/01/26 with a plan for routine outpatient follow-up in the respiratory clinic.
The ward nurse contacted the patient's GP on 08/01/26 to inform them of the patient's clinical progress and stability in preparation for discharge.
A final chest X-ray reviewed on 09/01/26 showed complete resolution of spontaneous pneumomediastinum with no subcutaneous emphysema or abnormalities.
The patient was cleared for discharge on 09/01/26 with no further imaging required.
